title: How Flirting Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss flirting as a form of body language and a kind of language studied by evolutionary psychologists, behavioral psychologists and anthropologists. Topics include why flirting matters for reproduction and mate selection, common flirting signs (using a name, complimenting, touching an arm or knee, leaning in, smiling), "proceptive" or Proteus-like ambiguous behavior that gives plausible deniability, sex differences in flirting, hip-to-waist ratio and fertility, Ronald Ebel-Eibl-style candid photography of couples in the 1970s and posture such as extended necks and puffed chests, a Hyatt hotel bar study, cross-cultural flirting confusion between Germans and Americans, and a Tulane study on flirting and women's workplace earnings and promotions. The episode closes with listener mail about guerrilla gardening and adverse possession.

segments.title: Opening banter and flirting demonstration
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter, Josh demonstrates a crude flirting line, and they introduce flirting as a language and blushing as a topic.

segments.title: Flirting as language and its role in reproduction
segments.summary: Flirting is described as body language studied as a language by evolutionary and behavioral psychologists and anthropologists. It lets people assess reproductive compatibility before sex, which keeps the population in check.

segments.title: Common flirting signs
segments.summary: The hosts list signs such as using a person's name often, complimenting, asking about interests, touching an arm or knee, leaning in close, and smiling. They joke that men often miss these cues.

segments.title: Proteus behavior and plausible deniability
segments.summary: Proteus behavior is described as ambiguous flirting, mostly by women, that sits between normal behavior and flirting and lets them back off if rejected. Men tend to flirt more aggressively, with intense eye contact and gesturing.

segments.title: Hip-to-waist ratio, posture and candid photo studies
segments.summary: Hip-to-waist ratio is linked to fertility, with ratios in the middle range considered most fertile. A researcher in the 1970s used a hidden camera to photograph flirting couples, finding patterns such as women extending their necks and men puffing out their chests. Facial symmetry and a prominent jaw are presented as signs of health and reproductive ability.

segments.title: Flirting research and cultural differences
segments.summary: Studies of flirting were mostly done in lounges, including a Hyatt hotel bar where researchers could predict from body language who would leave together. The hosts note there is no formula, and that cultures add their own interpretations, such as Germans and Americans misreading each other.

segments.title: Tulane study on flirting and workplace success
segments.summary: A Tulane University study of 164 women found that some used flirting to get ahead at work. Women who did not flirt reported higher salaries and were promoted about three times as often. The takeaway is that sexuality can be a short-term power source that cheapens personality.

segments.title: Closing advice on flirting
segments.summary: The hosts joke that making someone laugh is the best advice for flirting, and that good looks help.

segments.title: Listener mail on guerrilla gardening and property rights
segments.summary: A listener from Ashland, Wisconsin writes that in some areas long-term trespassing can give people rights to land, so planting flowers on someone's land could be a way to establish that. The hosts agree it is a good point and mention sending a T-shirt.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener mail at the show's email address and sign off.
